utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. You're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Before we adjourned on Friday, we were talking about your visit in Pelagicevo, and you told us that in the morning of the 9th of May, you went to Commander Nikolic and that Toso Tutnjevic drove you there. After that conversation, after this meeting with Commander Nikolic, did he give you some orders?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did Commander Nikolic order you to do?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the conversation that we had, Commander Nikolic said that he would undertake to talk about the incident with Messrs. Crni and Debeli, that he would also talk with Mr. Todorovic so that certain measures could be taken, and he told me, as transpired from the conversation, that it would be good if I went to Belgrade, call Makso Simeunovic, colonel, who at that time was retired. But I'm talking about Mr. Jugoslav Maksimovic, I'm sorry, colonel, who was retired, but who used to work in the security administration of the army of Yugoslavia and to try, through him, to convey the information to those most responsible in the security administration of the army of Yugoslavia so as to remove this problem from the agenda and see how it would be solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you -- and when did you go to Belgrade, if you did?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the conversation in Pelagicevo, in the command of the 17th Tactical Group, my driver, Toso Tutnjevic, and I returned to Samac. And later on, I took my private car - at that time I had a Golf - so I got into the car, put some of my -- of things there, because that was also an opportunity to visit my relatives in Belgrade and to see them, and I had agreed with the commander to stay a day longer so as to be able to see them, because at that time exactly my wife was in a hospital at Bezanijska Kosa because she was having a heart complaint. So that after I returned, as soon as I packed a few things, I immediately got into the car and left for Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You've already told us something about the meeting in the headquarters regarding the events in Crkvina, but now I'd like to ask you about some further details in this regard. First, can you tell us when you arrived with Jugoslav Maksimovic at the headquarters, what was the reaction of those present, when you told them about the crime in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, everybody was aghast, and nobody approved of that act. Mr. Jugoslav Maksimovic first took me to General Gligorijevic's office, and since I had testified about that during the previous days, after that meeting, General Aleksandar Maksimovic, Aco, also came and was present at this meeting. At that time, he was discharging the duty of the chief of the security administration of the army of Yugoslavia. And I deemed there is no need for me to repeat it once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: No, none whatsoever. Mr. Zaric, were you asked after these meetings to put together an official memo about the conversations that you had?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And that note, was it done?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The official note was written in one copy, and one only, and then it was retyped in that office, and I have to be honest and say that -- to those gentlemen, both Vasiljevic and General Gligorijevic, and even Colonel Maksimovic himself, who was present, and that I told them and asked them not to reveal my visit and to keep that note in a special way, as a secret, because I was afraid of those people. I was afraid they would take revenge on me and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe Mr. Zaric could clarify one thing, because according to what it says here in the transcript, and I listened very carefully to what he actually said, here he says on page 3, line 13: "The official note was written in one copy, and the only, and then it was retyped," which might suggest that some other copies have been made. So maybe this can be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, this note, will you tell us: How was it done technically?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technically, the secretary came into that office and to her directly - as I'm talking now, loudly, and clearly, as I'm testifying before this Trial Chamber - I dictated to her what I knew about the event most directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And when she took down your dictation, did you sign it then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed that official note exactly on the 9th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign that one copy only?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I signed only one copy, and that had been agreed to do it in one copy only, for purely security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So no other copies were made and you did not sign anything else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing except that one single copy of the official note, which took a page and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when you returned from Belgrade, did you report to Commander Nikolic about the results of your visit and tell him all that had happened?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Bosnia and Herzegovina, or rather, towards Samac and Pelagicevo, I returned exactly on the 11th of May, in the morning hours. From Belgrade, I directly went to the command of the 17th Tactical Group and told Colonel Stevan Nikolic and the security officer, Makso Simeunovic, how -- what was said during the meeting and what I had done there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zaric. Let us move on to another subject, the subject of isolation of a considerable number of citizens of Croat ethnicity in Crkvina. How did you learn about that, that a significant number of citizens of Croat ethnicity had been put in isolation in the village of Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt it in two ways. One part of that scene, that is, rounding up of people in trucks and taken to Crkvina, I saw with my own eyes, because it took place in front of my building. And secondly, in the public security station I had the opportunity on those days precisely to see a decision taken by the Crisis Staff to isolate the Croat people. That decision was in the office of the chief of the public security station, Mr. Todorovic, who, now and then, at that time, came to those premises, but one copy of that decision was also with people who worked in the criminal investigation department, that is, Mr. Milos Savic and Mr. Vlado Sarkanovic. So that what I saw with my own eyes, and when I saw this decision about isolation, then I became quite clear how that act had come about, to isolate people in the sense of the question that you asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zaric. And according to your knowledge, who rounded up women of Croat ethnicity in Bosanski Samac, and men too, and neighbouring villages, and put them in the stadium in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All my knowledge concerning the event indicated that it was exclusively within the jurisdiction of the police, the public security station in Bosanski Samac, and I was, for instance, the eyewitness to a case when the police came in a car, after that, that is, in a truck, fetched up in front of the building, and when a teacher, called Ruza, was already in the truck, and when Mrs. Jelena Kapetanovic boarded that truck, and only a day or two later a police vehicle took away two Muslim women too. So that at that moment, Croats were not the only ones who were going to that so-called isolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who guarded, who looked after those people and citizens in Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in Crkvina. I hadn't been to Crkvina. I had only heard that there was a large group of isolated people there from neighbouring Croat villages and the town of Samac, and I also had information that they were being guarded by members of the public security station in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, how long were people kept at the stadium in the village of Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It lasted about a couple of days. I really can't tell you how many exactly. But very soon after that -- and what is very soon afterward? Four or five days perhaps. And then the story went that people from Crkvina, from the big youth club that we called that, returned to their homes, and some men were isolated then in two gymnasiums. One belonged to the elementary school in Bosanski Samac and the other one was the gymnasium in the secondary school, again in Bosanski Samac. They are about a hundred metres away as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you ever go to this -- to either gymnasium of the elementary or the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to what went on there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing nice. From what I would hear, at certain points in time, when it occurred to Specials or some drunk policemen, they were exposed to ill-treatment, torture, degrading behaviour, and so on and so forth. And part of that story was directly told me by Djuro Prgomet, who is my friend, who is my daughter's father-in-law, who, for a while, was detained and isolated in those same premises where Croats were isolated, and he's also a Croat by origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what do you know, Mr. Zaric, about the village of Zasavica, and who was accommodated there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- the first time I learnt about the village of Zasavica was on the 26th of May, 1992, when, right next to that village, on the bank of the Bosna River, the first, I'd say, exchange of people of the population between the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we shall be talking about that exchange later on. But do you know whether some persons were accommodated there in that village?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, a more intensive arrival of non-Serb population to that village took place in August 1992. After a case which has to do with the flight of a large number of persons of Muslim ethnicity across the Sava River to the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who took relevant decisions, and who took those non-Serb families to the village of Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was all organised by the public security station in Bosanski Samac, headed by Mr. Stevan Todorovic. I know one fact regarding Zasavica, and that is that before the hostilities started in the territory of the Bosanski Samac municipality, a relatively large part of that population, at the invitation of the Crisis Staff in the municipality of Odzak, crossed the Bosna River into the territory of the municipality of Odzak. Because as far as I know, Zasavica is a village with 95 per cent of the Croat population. There were some 550 people who lived in that neighbourhood community, and more than one half of the population left the area before any incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. We shall leave now the village of Zasavica, but we shall return to it, rest assured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There was something in my respectful submission left unanswered by Mr. Zaric's answer. It's something which could normally be objectionable. That's the answer: "As far as I know, it was all organised by the public security station in Bosanski Samac, headed by Mr. Stevan Todorovic." Mr. Zaric hasn't given the basis for his knowledge, that is, how he knows it was Mr. Todorovic and what Mr. Todorovic actually did. Otherwise the answer would have been objectionable, but I didn't object because I thought he might explain it. So I'd asked that my learned friend clarify it with his client because it's appropriate to do so, in my submission, in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. That shouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you've understood what my learned friend wanted to know. How is it that you know that it was done by the public security station, headed by Stevan Todorovic? Did you see that, hear about that, read about it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was done in August, the transfer and rounding up of the population and the transfer to the territory of Zasavica, that was not something I had the opportunity to see with my own eyes, but I did have the opportunity to hear about it at those moments when, at that time, I was returning from Odzak to the Samac territory. That was when I was told that was done with the trucks, escorted by the police from the public security station. So I heard that it had been done in that way, and I had no opportunity to see that directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And in August, when this was being done, was Stevan Todorovic the chief of the public security station?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Mr. Stevan Todorovic discharged the duty almost until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you already said in your testimony that the army of Republika Srpska was founded on the 12th of May, 1992 and that the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 19th of May, 1992. What do you know regarding the departure of members of the army of Yugoslavia? Who left, and where did the officers and troops who left the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina or, in this case, the municipality of Bosanski Samac, originate from?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit, quite frankly, that that decision about the definitive pull-out of the Yugoslav People's Army on the 19th of May, 1992, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, was something that made me quite unhappy, because I knew that that meant the final extinction of a country which I loved. And I realised finally that with the departure of the Yugoslav People's Army from this territory, we'd start living under completely different conditions, and regrettably that is what happened. I know that the decision ordered that all the troops, officers, and NCOs in the Yugoslav People's Army who had been born in the territory of Serbia, Montenegro, or possibly some other republic, and who had, until then, been in the Yugoslav People's Army, had to leave the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is indeed what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, which military formations were formed in the army of Republika Srpska on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac, Pelagicevo, after the withdrawal of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of May, that is, on today's date in 1992, under a decision of the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the army of Republika Srpska was established. With the departure of the JNA on the 19th of May, a military transformation occurred of the armed forces which were on the territory of Republika Srpska. Instead of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA, which up to that moment had been the military defence component for the area of Bosanski Samac, among others, the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade was established, and all the detachments - and there were five infantry detachments at that time - were renamed and reorganised to make up infantry battalions which were later, of course, part of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: In these newly established military formations of the army of Republika Srpska, in the commands, in the battalions, the companies, squads, and so on, did people who had been born in Bosnia and Herzegovina stay?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade was Colonel Mico Djurdjevic, who was born in a village called Tisina, which is not far from the town of Samac and belongs to the municipality of Bosanski Samac. So he was born on the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When was Colonel Djurdjevic appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade and can you tell us when this happened how old he was and whether you know anything about him as a man and a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly how old he was, but it was between 50 and 60 years of age. And according to my estimation, he was a very strong, courageous, stout-hearted officer, and a very calm, disciplined, and moderate officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When Commander Djurdjevic was appointed commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, did he take any measures within the sphere of his competence to improve the situation on the territory?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he convene a meeting in Pelagicevo, the village where the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade was located?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A few days afterwards, that is, about five or six days after his arrival, Colonel Djurdjevic was active on two fronts. As far as I was able to observe, one of these fronts was organising the brigade command and setting up the organisation of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade in such a way that one could tell who was at the top and who was at the bottom. And as for the second front I mentioned, I thought he worked very well on collecting certain information in order to determine what the situation of this unit was, what its state was, the unit that was now called the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. About five days later, Colonel Mico Djurdjevic convened a meeting of prominent persons, and this was held in a room in Pelagicevo. The persons who attended the meeting included almost all the commanders of the battalions, their assistants for security and moral guidance, all the commanders of other independent units within the scope of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, part of the new command that had already been inaugurated by him within the 2nd Posavina Brigade, and the most responsible people from the political life of the municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo under foundation. This was approximately the composition of the people who attended that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I participated in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was there on behalf of the civilian authorities of the municipalities of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am certain that on behalf of Bosanski Samac municipality, the meeting was attended by Mr. Blagoje Simic, as the president of the Crisis Staff; by Mr. Milan Simic; Mr. Stevan Todorovic; maybe there was Mr. Milos Bogdanovic, but I'm not sure; and Bozo Ninkovic. But the first three men I mentioned were there. I'm certain of that. And on behalf of Pelagicevo, there was Dusan Tanaskovic, Milan Milicic, and Mirko Dragic, who then held two posts, one in the military and the other political, because he was the president of the Serbian Democratic Party there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What did Colonel Djurdjevic, the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, say at that meeting? If you can summarise it briefly, just mention the topics he discussed, and what did he want from the military and from the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He drew attention to the gravity of the situation we were in after the departure of the JNA from that area, and he used a saying to the effect that we should rely on our own strength now, meaning that we were now the local representatives of the Serbian people, whether we were in the military or politicians, and that it was up to us to organise and take over the territory and the defence of the Serbian people in that area. He also drew attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Zaric. We have a comment on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: There is something here in the transcript that Mr. Zaric didn't say, on page 13, line 9, 8 and 9, that "it was up to us to organise and take over the territory." This is not the words that Mr. Zaric said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did he say you should take over the territory or that you should defend the territory?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said: Whether we are speaking of the military or of politicians, it is our task to organise ourselves in such a way as to ensure a defence component so as to preserve the territory on which the Serbian people live. That was the context of what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What else did Colonel Djurdjevic say at that meeting? Did he ask that the civilian authorities should deal with civilian matters and the military with military matters, or something like that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so. It became evident from what he was saying that he had taken stock of the situation very well and he didn't want to conceal this from any of us. He drew attention to the fact that there had been kinds of behaviour that were not in accordance with military rules and discipline, and that politicians had interfered in military matters, and vice versa, and that this was intertwined. He was very explicit about this, saying that, as commander, he would advocate exclusively that the military do its job and take responsibility for the defence of the territory, and that he would not allow any groups - and he referred especially to the volunteers from Serbia - that he would not allow them to act as they wanted, in line with the information he had. And he said it had to be clear that what was with the army had to be under the control of the military, and what was in the police had to be under the control of the police, and everything else outside of that were paramilitaries and parapolice and would not be allowed to remain on the territory. He said he would not allow politics to interfere in the personnel policy of the military, and he also said that the military could not psychologically influence political standpoints and attitudes in that area. That would be a summary of what he said in front of all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe the transcript was not quite accurate. Here on page 14, lines 18 and 19, and 17 as well, "military could not psychologically influence political standpoints." Could not -- well, what Mr. Zaric was referring to is certain military pressure on politicians to meet the demands of the army, and the way it is said now, some psychological influence, doesn't sound quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I mean, in actual fact it comes to the same thing. It's the military influencing political standpoints that also could include applying pressure on the political leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, on that occasion, did Commander Djurdjevic say, or rather, ask, that the volunteers should either be placed under the command of the military or the police, or, if they refused that, that they could go to Serbia over the Drina River?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely as you said. That's what he said, very decidedly, and that's what he advocated at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what did the other participants in the meeting say? Did they support the commander? Did they oppose his intentions and measures?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the discussion, several battalion commanders took part, first of all. As far as I can remember, the politicians did not take the floor, but when the colonel was summarising what had taken place, as to whether all of us present in the room agreed with what he had said and what I have testified to, there was no one present at the meeting who raised any objections to these firm and clear standpoints taken by Commander Djurdjevic. On the basis of this, I and many others concluded that unanimity had been achieved concerning the standpoints put forward by the commander at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And how did the meeting end, the meeting with Colonel Djurdjevic, the commander?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say that it ended in a good atmosphere, at least in my view. Perhaps after the withdrawal of the JNA, for the first time there was a sense of relief among most of us, and with that meeting we seemed to have surmounted the psychological crisis we had been undergoing, that is, our anxiety about what would happen in the future. So this meeting ended well and had a very positive effect on all the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know what happened to Colonel Djurdjevic, the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, a few days after this meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know. About seven days later, as regards Colonel Djurdjevic and some relations, the situation went wrong. It turned around. And the impression I had had of unity, when the meeting in Pelagicevo ended, had in fact been only a pretense of support, and afterwards commander Djurdjevic was replaced in circumstances that I think are special.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know whether Commander Djurdjevic, before he was replaced, attended a meeting, and where that meeting was held?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was at a meeting. The meeting was organised in the Toplana, in the heat-generating plant, where the headquarters of the Bosanski Samac municipality Crisis Staff was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who invited Commander Djurdjevic to that meeting in the heating plant where the headquarters of the Crisis Staff of the Bosanski Samac municipality was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a conversation that I had later on with Mr. Djurdjevic, I learnt that he had been invited to the Crisis Staff by Mr. Blagoje Simic and Mr. Stevan Todorovic. I was one of the people who was present at part of that meeting, and I witnessed a scenario that took place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What part of the meeting were you present at, and who brought you to the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was brought to the meeting by my driver, Toso Tutnjevic, and I had just been at the front lines, the defence lines of what was already the 5th Battalion, in its area of responsibility, and I had received information that I should report urgently to the Crisis Staff, where Commander Djurdjevic was attending a meeting, and that the commander of the 5th Infantry Battalion, Mr. Jovo Savic, had already gone to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who ordered you to go to that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty communications officer in the 4th Detachment told me that Commander Jovo Savic had sent word that I was to go to the meeting in the Crisis Staff, urgently, and that the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, Colonel Mico Djurdjevic, was already there. On the basis of this information, I went to the heating plant by car and came to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you used the expression "the 4th Detachment," and just before you mentioned the 5th Battalion. What unit was it at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the 5th Infantry Battalion, because after the new establishment, that was the name it was given, after the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we have already explained this. If there is a slip of the tongue, we will correct it. Don't worry about this. And when you arrived at the meeting in the heating plant, where the Crisis Staff was, who did you see there at the meeting? Who was present?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the president of the Crisis Staff was full, full of people. Apart from the commander, Mico Djurdjevic, as the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, there was also my commander, the commander of the 5th Infantry Battalion, Captain Jovo Savic. Of the people from the Crisis Staff, there was Mr. Blagoje Simic, Mr. Stevan Todorovic, Bozo Ninkovic, but I don't know whether at that point in time he held any special post. Then there was Simeun Simic, and in my estimation, about ten lads in military camouflage uniforms, with weapons. They were all in the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you recollect whether Savo Popovic also attended the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible that Mr. Popovic was there as well, but I'm not a hundred per cent sure right now. It is possible, though, that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who chaired the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wish to say that I came to the meeting, and there was a certain atmosphere there. When I entered, I was assigned a small space with a chair, and at the time the speaker was Mr. Stevan Todorovic, which doesn't mean that he chaired the meeting as well. However, when I got into the office, he was the one who was delivering the speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what transpired during the meeting, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic, in his typical style, and in my opinion without any respect for the others, turned to Colonel Mico Djurdjevic and said to him that he had received information to the effect that the army, and especially people from the special battalion, as it was called at the time, were not pleased with the attitude that he took as commander, and that he, as commander, was not trusted by the Serb population in the Samac municipality, and should he fail to change his attitude, the Serb people could pay dearly for that consequence, and that certain lack of unity could come out of that in the area. This is what I remember Mr. Todorovic saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you also mentioned that there were some men there who were armed and wearing camouflage uniforms. Do you remember anybody in that group, anybody in particular?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I remember Mr. Aco Jankovic, for example, who was quite rough and insolent at the meeting. I remember when he addressed even the president of the Crisis Staff, and later on me as well, and said: Why is it that somebody who doesn't have to wear a military uniform - and at that time Mr. Blagoje Simic had a military jacket, a camouflage type, and I had a similar one as well - and then he turned to me and said: And people like Zaric, why would they need a military uniform? So as I said, he was quite rough, and he made it known that should Mr. Mico Djurdjevic continue acting in this manner, that the volunteers, these major warriors, if I can call them that, would leave the area, and that with them the area would be also deserted by those who attended training with them, and that that could bring about negative consequences among the troops and among the people. I remember one of those people who took the floor. His name was Aco Jankovic. And in addition to him, there was Cedo Lukic there as well, who had attended special meeting. Then there was another lad from Gajevo, whose name I cannot remember. Later on, he unfortunately was killed. I think the name was Lukic. I think he attended the meeting as well. So all in all, those were the men who had attended the training, which prior to the war was kept secret by Mr. Todorovic and some other people who had sent them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And in this tense atmosphere, did Commander Djurdjevic give some kind of a proposal to Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't wish to repeat myself, but I, and perhaps quite a large number of people who had occasion to hear and to see what was the attitude of Mr. Djurdjevic as commander, and I have to say that he's a very calm, moderate person - he, having assessed the situation, said the following: This is not an atmosphere in which such serious discussions can take place. And then he suggested to Mr. Blagoje that all of us who were in the room should leave it and to have Mr. Blagoje Simic, Stevan Todorovic, and himself only remain in the room. And following that, this is exactly what took place: All of us left the room, while the three of them remained there in the office of the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody else enter the room subsequently, the office of the president of the Crisis Staff, while the meeting, including Djurdjevic, Simic, and Todorovic, still went on?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the lower part of that building, which is called the heating plant, there was a mini restaurant where some of us sat. Some of the people were in front of the building. And after about an hour, perhaps even less than that, after about an hour following our leaving the room, a car came with Mr. Crni in it, and then he entered the room with those three gentlemen in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How long did that meeting in the office of the president of the Crisis Staff go on for?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An hour at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you learn following the end of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first to come down the stairs was Mr. Stevan Todorovic, who was in a very good mood and quite talkative. He came down to the mini restaurant where all of us were sitting. He said: Everything is over. Commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade is Crni. He didn't say Dragan Djordjevic. He just said Crni. He said commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade is Crni. Everything has been agreed. There will be no problems. He came to Mr. Jovo Savic [as interpreted] and to me to congratulate us on the appointment of the new commander, whereas I considered this to be a slap in our face.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Just one word in transcript, page 21, line 14. He came to Mr. Jovo Savic and to me. Mr. Zaric was referring to Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, truly become commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What is your opinion about his military qualifications and skills as commander of a brigade, and I mean Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not have the skills to command a unit of that size. However, he was a brave soldier and he could have led a small sabotage unit. I do not deny that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did he have any military education? Did he hold a rank, a military rank?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I knew then, and as far as I learned later, he had no qualifications whatsoever. He was an ordinary soldier. He had only attended this special training based on which he received the status of the instructor or inspector within the special police forces.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before the answer, the question was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, who was appointment chief of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade within the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Colonel -- Lieutenant Colonel Dencic, who was acting commander of the east Bosnia Corps, officially appointed Mr. Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, then many of us learned for the first time that his actual name was Dragan Djordjevic. Up until that time, we only knew him as Crni, which was his nickname. When, after two or three days following this meeting at the Crisis Staff, he received an official decision appointing him commander and awarding him the rank of lieutenant colonel, which is something that can happen anywhere in the world, therefore, then Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, appointed Srecko Radovanovic chief of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. His nickname was Debeli. And he and Crni had come together with the other Specials on the 11th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you remember who was appointed commander of the military police company at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovanovic, Zvjezdan, was appointed company commander of the military police. He was one of the Specials that had come from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, following these changes within the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, was commander of the 5th Battalion within this 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade also replaced? And now I'm talking of Jovo Savic.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that event very clearly. After the arrival of Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, as commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, Captain Jovo Savic was replaced. He used to be commander of the 5th Infantry Battalion. And he was -- the person who replaced him was Mr. Radovic, whom I considered a military dissident. And at the time I was collecting information that would lead to him being disciplined, due to some of the acts he had committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mladen Radovic have any rank, officer's rank, or was he a non-commissioned officer?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was a sergeant at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, and who removed Mr. Jovo Savic, Captain Jovo Savic, from his post as commander of the 5th Infantry Battalion and replaced him with Mladen Radovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decision replacing the old commander and appointing the new commander was the decision passed by Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, and Captain Savic was the one who relayed to me certain details regarding that. After he was replaced, he told me about what had happened in the premises of the department store, which is where Mr. Savic went pursuant to summons from Mr. Stevan Todorovic and where Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, shortly thereafter, did you travel to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Shortly after these events I went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Who asked you to go to Belgrade, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Blagoje Simic asked me to go to Belgrade. It was a telephone call that came in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and the accused please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that I should be in Belgrade the following day, due to certain tasks and things that needed to be done. When he spoke with me on the phone, he didn't give me the reasons. I told him that I didn't mind going there because I considered that to be an opportunity to visit my family as well. That was my thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, who else went to Belgrade with you, and how did you travel there? What transportation means did you use?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Blagoje told me that I was to go to Belgrade, I asked him what were the arrangements, when we were to leave, and so on. Since Mr. Blagoje Simic and I lived in the same building but not in the same parts of the building, he told me that sometime around 6.00 I should be in front of the building and that the car would come to fetch us. That's exactly how it was. It was Blagoje who went to Belgrade with me. We were driven in a police car by Mr. Stevan Todorovic and Mr. Miroslav Tadic came with us as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was there somebody awaiting you in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Belgrade, by a building which was considered to be a government building of the Republika Srpska in Belgrade, in front of the building we were met by Mr. Milos Bogdanovic, who at the time was municipal secretary for National Defence in Bosanski Samac municipality. In the car with him was his wife and two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you met with Milos Bogdanovic, was there a verbal conflict that broke out there and then; and if so, please tell us who was involved.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not stay long there in front of that building, as Mr. Todorovic had told us that we should leave as soon as possible in order to attend a meeting at the republic Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, because there were some people there that he had and that we had to see. Therefore, he just suggested for Milos Bogdanovic to transfer from the car in which he was to the car in which all of us were. Therefore, Milos joined us, whereas his wife and children remained at the parking place, waiting there for him, because Milos believed that he would be able to join his family shortly. In the car, as we were driving towards the centre of Belgrade, Milos Bogdanovic put a question to Mr. Todorovic in front of all of us. He said: Stevo, what were your orders all about, the orders on arresting people in Gorice? Yesterday I barely managed to pass, and were it not for Debeli - and by this he referred to Srecko Radovanovic, who at the time was chief of staff - therefore, were it not for him, I would not have been able to go to Belgrade. You had ordered to your policemen at the checkpoint in Gorice to arrest me. I saw Mr. Simo Zaric, Miroslav Tadic, Jovo Savic, Fadil Topcagic, and Savo Popovic on that list of yours of men to be arrested. Those were approximately the names of people who, pursuant to Stevan Todorovic's order, should have been arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what happened after that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevo said that this was some kind of a pre-emptive message and that he did not consider it to be terribly important. However, I have to say that when I heard about this in the car, when I heard that my name was on the list of people to be arrested, a very fierce verbal conflict broke out between myself and Mr. Todorovic, and in that altercation and argument, while we were arguing, we arrived into the yard of the Republic Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And how did that conflict calm down, the conflict involving you and Bogdanovic, on one side, and Stevan Todorovic on the other side?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only owing to Mr. Blagoje Simic. He said something along these lines: If we are unable to calm down, and if we are unable to overcome this arguments, then we should get back into the car and return to Samac immediately. That's what Blagoje said in the yard of that building, once we got there. I have to say that after that, we calmed down a little bit, because we had arrived in front of the building and we were to attend a meeting that seemed to have been organised by Mr. Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have a meeting in the building of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Todorovic was the only one who left the car while it was parked in the yard of that building. The four of us remained in the car. He went to the reception desk and talked to the duty person and was told that Mr. Frenki was not there and that we could not attend the meeting that he had planned, but should rather go to see Mr. Andjelko Maslic, who at the time had a post in the federal government of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you go to see Mr. Andjelko Maslic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We went in a car to the new Belgrade area, where the building of the federal government was at the time. Mr. Andjelko Maslic is somebody who was originally from our area, from the area of Bosanski Samac municipality, and he was the last secretary of the presidency of the federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did all of you go to see Mr. Andjelko Maslic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What did you talk about with Mr. Andjelko Maslic on that occasion when you visited him?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there were several current topics to be discussed with Mr. Andjelko Maslic. The most important topic, as far as I can remember, dealt with the fate of certain requests, concerning which the Crisis Staff of Samac wrote to the federal government, and it had to do with the fate of Serbs that had been arrested and detained in Odzak municipality. We spoke to Mr. Andjelko Maslic whether anything else could be done regarding that, whether any other contacts could be used to do something about the fate of those detained people. And the other topic that we discussed was the fate of a large number of refugees from the territory of Samac municipality who, according to our information, were stationed in two or three areas, locations, around Belgrade. I know that a large number of refugees of all nationalities from Samac were housed around Bezanijska Kosa, another group near Pancevo, and there was a third location where they were housed. I also remember well that Mr. Blagoje, just like all of us, insisted and pleaded with Mr. Maslic to see what he could do to assist, through the Red Cross and other institutions, to see what he could do for the people from our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it is time for our break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We shall take our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Before we proceed, the Trial Chamber would like to address the Prosecution. The demographer's report was filed on the 8th of May, and the Trial Chamber wanted to find out from the Prosecution when they will be able to reply, to indicate whether they want the expert for cross-examination. We were thinking that maybe you would be able to reply by Friday this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't think that should be a problem at all, if Your Honours please, and I'm quite happy to put in a reply by Friday. That should be no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can have the reply orally, unless there are some other details you wish to put in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd be very grateful if we could do that. That would save a lot of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll -- perhaps Friday morning or afternoon, depending on whether we have morning or afternoon sessions, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think by morning so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well. I'll make it clear on Friday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If the Prosecution indicates that they would like to cross-examine, the Trial Chamber was thinking that - this was addressed to the Defence, especially Mr. Lukic, who appears to be in touch with this expert - that she should attend court on the 26th of May, that is, in two weeks' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not think this will cause any problems. Independently of the Prosecution's request and decision of the Trial Chamber, I have already asked the Victims and Witnesses Unit to prepare the visa for Mrs. Radovanovic, and I think that it will be granted. At the time I was discussing with her the schedule in principle, she said that she could come in May any time, except that she would need to know two or three days earlier because of her other commitments. So if we accept that it will be the 26th of May, that will be fine, and I can, if it is so decided, I shall inform her to reserve that particular time and she'll come. There will be no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be better to inform her of that date right away, and then subject to confirmation as to which position the Prosecution will take by Friday, so that she can clear her diary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, by all means. That is the best option. So I'll let her know today, and as far as she is concerned, there will be no problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before the break we were talking about the meeting at Mr. Andjelko Maslic's. So how did this meeting with Mr. Andjelko Maslic end?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd say that it ended in a completely normal atmosphere among people who knew one another and who had to discuss two or three serious subjects. But to my mind, it ended very correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. Did you go to any other meeting after the meeting with Mr. Andjelko Maslic ended?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And where did you go, and who else went with you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the meeting, we went to Zemun, which is a part of Belgrade, to the main building of the command of the air force and AAD of Yugoslavia. And when we set off from the platform in front of that building which housed government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and where we had been at the meeting with Mr. Andjelko Maslic, Stevan Todorovic, whether in jest or deliberately, said, in front of everybody: Now I'm taking you to my central office. That was his interjection, his comment. And after ten minutes or so, because it wasn't far away, we fetched up in front of this building of the command of the AF and AAD of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, who received you there in that building of the AF and AAD command?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the office to which we went upstairs, after, of course, the procedure of reporting at the reception desk, we were welcomed -- well, they -- he was introduced as General Gajic. General Bajic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was at the time Chief of Staff of the AF, AAD of Yugoslavia, so I'm referring to General Bajic. There was also with him Colonel -- his name escapes me right now, even though it is very familiar. But I'll remember it as I testify. And Mr. Todorovic greeted them, particularly cordially and warm-heartedly, and from this I concluded that they had known each other from before. Then we entered a large conference room, with a large conference table with several chairs. In that room there were already two men in police uniforms, and they merely introduced themselves, saying they were coming from the federal secretariat of the interior. That was that I do not remember their names, but as we shook hands, Colonel Jeremic -- now it's come to me, I'm sorry. I have just remember, it was Colonel Jeremic who was the PR man for a man in the security department of the special service of the AF, AAD of Yugoslavia. We entered this room, all five of us. We had -- we partook of coffee there, and a spontaneous discussion started after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before that, had you ever met General Bajic and Colonel Jeremic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never met them, nor, to be quite honest, had I ever heard of them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was discussed at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at first there was the usual atmosphere. Stevan Todorovic perhaps took the lead and made some general assessments about the state of things on the front line in the area of Bosanski Samac, and during the meeting, after that atmosphere, a man turned up and everybody received him with a certain respect and stood up. He was wearing civilian clothes and he merely introduced himself as Frenki.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn the real name of that person, and what post did he hold?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that only after I arrived here in The Hague. That is, before that, I had no idea. And when he introduced himself as Frenki and said he came from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, that was the only identification we heard about him at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: But later on did you find out what his name was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's called Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, at that meeting, was there any mention of Dragan Djordjevic, called Crni, and who raised that topic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan Djordjevic did come up in the discussion. I think that it was after Mr. Frenki arrived it became the chief topic at the meeting and the chief topic of the discussion conducted then. Mr. Blagoje Simic, during those discussion, when the term came to talk about Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, said, more or less, that this was an individual who enjoyed outstanding trust of the combatants in the area of Samac, that he was a brave guy, and that that was the impression he left amongst the troops. After him, Stevan Todorovic made charisma out of Mr. Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, as said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain what you mean by this.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he approximately said that new time gives birth to new heroes and that he, simply put -- for the Serbian Bosnian people he had become an idol, that he had become a hero, and that it had become inconceivable to wage any further struggle without him and that that was one of the chief reasons why he had been appointed and was currently performing the duty of the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade in Samac. And among other things, he said how valiant he was, how brave he was, how intrepid he was, and he said that he had to all intents and purposes become the idol of the Serbian people and that the struggle could not be fought without him. That was about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Simatovic say anything on that occasion concerning the abilities and qualifications of Mr. Dragan Djordjevic, Crni?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, very briefly. Mr. Frenki Simatovic commented on those thoughts that we had heard before, and I remember well when Mr. Frenki said, approximately this: I think that Crni is not a man of a calibre allowing him to lead a brigade. He does not possess those abilities. His level is such that he could lead perhaps a unit of a sabotage nature. But, he said, if it is your decision to have him as a brigade commander, then you need another team of people in the command of the brigade who are qualified -- who are properly qualified, because Crni can't even read maps. And I remember that very well indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zaric. How long, as this meeting went on, did General Bajic talk over the telephone with somebody?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. General Bajic, after all this talk and requests put forward by Mr. Todorovic, and invitation to all of us present there to voice our official opinions as to what we thought about Mr. Crni, and as we were doing that, I think that Mr. Miroslav Tadic was the only one who wasn't in the room with us there as we were discussing this, because as we were discussing it, Mr. Miroslav Tadic left the room for a moment to meet a high-ranking officer in the AF and AAD Yugoslavia who was a relative of his and who was a pilot in the air force of Yugoslavia and was born in Novi Grad. And I know that Miroslav Tadic at some point went out of the room, and then Milos Bogdanovic presumably assessed the situation - I don't know how - and said that he had nothing against Crni being the brigade commander. And to be quite honest, it was fortunate for me that before me Mr. Frenki took the floor and said what he said. That is what I've just told you about. And when Mr. Todorovic insisted, said: Let's hear what Mr. Zaric has to say about Mr. Crni. Your Honours, at that moment, I assessed my position, and I wish to say that all I said was: In view of the thoughts expressed by Mr. Frenki, that is, that Crni was not up to the job and so on, that I agreed with that appraisal, but that in principle I had nothing against Mr. Crni discharging that duty. The words I uttered were the result of my assessment of the situation rather than my private opinion and appraisal of his capabilities. But it is up to the Honourable Court to make the final assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you have been talking now about things that I had already prepared about that, but you didn't answer the question that I asked you, and that was whether General Bajic, during that meeting, talked with somebody over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After this discussion that I've told you about, General Bajic said: Right now I'm going to call General Mladic. Now did he say my class? When he says "class," then in the Yugoslav People's Army and perhaps in other armies of the world, this usually means people belonging to a particular generation when they graduate from the military academy. So he stood up, opened the door, left the room, and there one of the officers, because there was a small office in front of this one, an officer provided a connection for him and he had a conversation with General Ratko Mladic so clearly that we could roughly hear what General Bajic was saying. We don't know what General Mladic was saying, but we know the approximate words which General Bajic uttered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did you conclude from these words that General Bajic was talking with General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And as he was talking with General Mladic, what kind of a conversation was it? Could you learn something from the manner in which you were listening to this conversation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, when General Bajic let Mladic know that there was some kind of a delegation of representatives from Samac and that we were allegedly supporting Mr. Crni, and so on, then General Mladic said something and replied. And after that, I remember well General Bajic saying: I know that Mladic, but he was appointed by Dencic. As if Lieutenant or Colonel Dencic who was discharging the duty had appointed Crni as the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. And then a conversation ensued. Right. So that's the situation. Let them see how he will turn out to be. And that was the end of the talk and the conversation between General Bajic and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And then General Bajic returned to the room. Did he say anything?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. So help me. My classmate seems to be angry. But, he said, or at least that is how I understood it, he should now take you to task. And this word, "take you to task," means to tell him some -- to criticise him, to say something daring. That is how I understood -- that is how I saw this word, "take to task," to Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did Blagoje Simic go and take over the connection?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Blagoje Simic went. He greeted General Mladic. They did not talk long. Blagoje was explaining some attitude concerning Mr. Crni, that is, that he was enjoying this courage amongst the soldiers, as said. And General Mladic replied something, and later on Blagoje Simic told us what was General Mladic's reaction within that context. And he said: Right, General. We shall bear this in mind, as we are about to do. Thank you. It was only two or three sentences which we could overhear through this open door, and Mr. Blagoje, I have to say, returned to this office rather flushed. One could see that this conversation with Ratko Mladic didn't make him particularly happy, that he was quite upset about it, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did Blagoje Simic tell you after all that? What was the conversation between him and General Mladic about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, simply, and in a nutshell, Blagoje said that General Mladic had said to him: Mr. President, you are the municipal mayor, mobilise the people to feed the army, take care of other things which have to do with the people, and don't meddle with the army and their personnel policy there. At least that is what I understood to have been the message, as Blagoje put it to us. And I also remember when Blagoje told him that he had been appointed by Colonel Dencic, that he had not been appointed by the Crisis Staff. So that would be this story in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And how long did this meeting take? How long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not particularly long, because people had other commitments. And after this whole story, I don't know if we had that one coffee or more, or did we finish our discussions then and left this building of the AF and AAD. Whatever the case, we did not stay there much longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any other meetings with official representatives of the government of Serbia or the army or somebody?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody else. I know well that we only went back to that first building that we had gone to when we had arrived in the morning, and in that car, Mr. Milos Bogdanovic's wife and his two children were still sitting in that car. It was already in the afternoon hours. So that Milos Bogdanovic stayed on with his family, and Mr. Blagoje, Mr. Todorovic, Mr. Miroslav Tadic, and I returned to Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, now we shall move on to the subject of exchanges. What can you tell us about the exchange of the 26th of May, 1992, near the village of Zasavica, by the Bosna River, which you have already mentioned in your testimony? How did you find out about that exchange?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two before that exchange, there was a lot of talk in the town of Samac about it, and it just happened that I learnt that such an exchange was afoot and that representatives of the International Red Cross were involved in it, and I think that the first information about that exchange I received in a spontaneous conversation with Mr. Tadic. But some other people also knew about that exchange, so that it was not difficult to learn that this exchange was being organised by the International Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you present during the exchange? Will you tell us: Where were you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was present at the exchange. It took place at the outskirts of the village of Zasavica, on the bank of the Bosna, which separates the municipalities of Samac and Odzak. On that occasion, from what I could see, there were many people, I'd say, who, either out of curiosity or because somebody from the other side was coming to them, were onlookers at that exchange, and the vehicles which brought persons to be exchanged had taken a side road; that is, they didn't come through the village of Zasavica. They just took a side road, fetched up some three or four hundred metres away, not far from the bank of the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Why were you there, and in what capacity were you there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had received information that the exchange which the Red Cross was in charge of would involve members of my family and relatives arriving from the municipality of Odzak, and this was the main reason I was among those present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any assignment in that exchange?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was simply an onlooker, someone waiting for his own relatives to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think there is an error in the transcript, page 38, line 23. Mr. Zaric said the information that the Red Cross had at its disposal. It says here: "Which the Red Cross was in charge of." He said that the information that was at the disposal of the Red Cross was that his relatives would be arriving. So could this be clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: How did you, Mr. Zaric, get the information that some relatives of yours would be exchanged in this exchange organised by the International Red Cross? Who did you get the information from?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally got this information in the Red Cross, because I went there when I heard that they were coming. I went to their offices. And one of the women there showed me the list, and I saw a large number of my relatives and friends, all of them elderly, that would be coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you went to the Red Cross, did you go to the municipal Red Cross of Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the municipal Red Cross that had its headquarters in the pensioners' club.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. In relation to the question before, at line 14: How did you, Mr. Zaric, get the information that some relatives of yours would be exchanged in this exchange organised by the International Red Cross, with respect, there's been no evidence from this witness that it was in fact organised by the International Red Cross. A few moments ago, Mr. Zaric said it was easy to learn that it had been. In my submission, if he's going to say that and try to assert that it's an established fact, that it was in fact organised by the International Red Cross, that's the ICRC, Mr. Zaric has to tell the Trial Chamber the source of his information that enables him to so conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic. You've heard what Mr. Re has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have heard what my learned friend has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on page 38, line 5, Mr. Zaric was giving his answer, "exchange was afoot and the representatives of the International Red Cross were involved in it." I found it in the transcript, so this is not quite accurate what Mr. Re just said. Mr. Zaric actually did mention International Red Cross as the organiser of this exchange, on page 38, line 5 and 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, but I thought that the Prosecution would still want to know how he came to know that the International Red Cross were involved at all. The question still remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, how did you learn that there would be an exchange and that this exchange was being organised and carried out by the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that one of the people who gave me this information was Mr. Miroslav Tadic, from whom I heard that the International Red Cross was getting involved and that there would be an exchange and that certain talks had been held with the local Red Cross in Bosanski Samac. This is the information I received, and about two days before this information [as interpreted], this was generally known. And on the 26th, in the morning, I went to the Red Cross, and from one of the women - I think it was Mrs. Petkovic or perhaps Mrs. Jovanovic, who were working there - I got a list. I saw the list drawn up by the local Red Cross of people arriving from the municipality of Odzak to the municipality of Bosanski Samac. This is why I decided to be present at the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... For the transcript on page 41, line 8. Mr. Zaric actually said: "About two days before this exchange," not this information, "this was generally known." It was generally known two days before the exchange actually happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I renew my objection to Mr. Zaric saying that he knew that the International Red Cross had organised the exchange. The explanation he has just given in response to my learned friend's question: How did you know it was organised, was Mr. Tadic had told me that the ICRC was "getting involved." And there's a large difference between organising and getting involved. And unless Mr. Zaric can give a better basis for his knowledge, for his conclusion of "organised," I object to that evidence going in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think from Mr. Zaric's point of view, besides informing the Trial Chamber that he was given that information by Mr. Miroslav Tadic, he hasn't said anything further. Yes, you can continue, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in the area where the exchange was to be carried out, that is, in the vicinity of the River Bosna, where were you standing, and who were you with, when you reached that spot?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stood there with a group of citizens, perhaps 20 or 30 metres away from the trucks, when the trucks arrived with a police escort. And among these citizens, there were people from Trnjak, Donja Dubica, Novi Grad, who either lived in the Bosanski Samac municipality or had arrived there before the war, and they wanted to show that they cared about their people. So there was quite a large group of citizens there looking on and observing the course of the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This group of people whom you have just described, this was the group you were standing with, if I understood you correctly, 20 metres away from the trucks, in which the persons participating in the exchange were?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You have just said that this group of people, which included you, was some 20 or 30 metres away from the trucks where the people to be exchanged were. How far were you from the bank of the River Bosna, where the exchange actually took place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three hundred to four hundred metres, in my estimation, because there was a winding path leading to that spot and we couldn't see, but the bank was some 300 to 400 metres away from the spot where we were standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, was Teodor Tutnjevic among that group?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I'm not sure. I can't remember now. It's possible that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Zaric, come to the village of Zasavica together with Teodor Tutnjevic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that he drove me there, so he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you were able to see the trucks. Could you explain what the procedure was for the exchange? Who was beside the trucks? How did events unfold?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were policemen from the public security station next to the trucks, and when the people got off the trucks, their names were read out by a representative of the ICRC, next to whom, I remember well, was one of the policemen. The representative of the ICRC could not read the names properly because the local names are difficult to pronounce, and the policeman who was observing the representative [Realtime transcript read in error "president"] of the ICRC reading out the names, after five or six names, he would, if the representative of the ICRC calling out the names had mispronounced the name, then the policeman would correct it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just for clarification: It says on page 43, line 19 that it was the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross who was reading out the names. I think maybe we should check with Mr. Zaric to see who actually it was.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter said "representative."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard, representative. It's just the way it is typed. So it was representative, actually. So just proceed with your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, is it right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "representative."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when the group was formed, where did it go?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
