utterances.text: When a group of five or six people was formed, one of the policemen would lead those people down the path, in the direction of the River Bosna, where the exchange was carried out. In the meantime, we observing the situation were informed that on the bank of the River Bosna there was a woman who was also a representative of the ICRC, and another representative, as far as I knew, there were three of them all together, who were registering certain things and directly conducting the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, from the spot where you were standing, were you able to see that woman and those other representatives carrying out the exchange on the bank of the River Bosna?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. From the spot where we were standing, we couldn't, or at least I couldn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: On that occasion while you were there, in one of the groups of people to be exchanged, was there someone who approached you and asked you something?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us who it was and how this happened.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was approached by Mr. Andrija Petric, a man who knew me, and I have to say that I also knew Mr. Petric from before, and probably in passing, when he was supposed to go down toward the River Bosna, he said he wanted to see me. And these people said to me that Andrija Petric wanted to see me and tell me something, and of course I approached Andrija to see him and to see what he wanted from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Andrija Petric ask you to do?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andrija only said that he did not want to go to the other side, that his wife and children were remaining on this side, and it so happened that Andrija Petric was married to a woman whose mother was born in Trnjak, where I come from, where I was born, and I said to Mr. Petric, when he got to the banks of the River Bosna, where the representatives of the ICRC were, that he should tell them that he did not want to cross over to the other side. There was nothing else I could do to help him. And he said to me: Is there anyone still there? Is there somebody else there? Because he thought that the man whose name -- who had called out their names was doing what he was doing and that would be the end of it as far as the procedure went.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you explain to Mr. Petric what your status was there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said to him: Andrija, I don't decide about anything here, but my advice to you is, because I had heard from what the people there were saying that there was a small table there, a sort of camp table, on which there was a piece of paper, and that the representatives of the ICRC were there and that people were being asked as to whether they wanted to go or not. So I said to him: Tell the representatives of the ICRC who were there that you don't want to go, and I think everything will be all right. That was my suggestion to Mr. Petric.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to whether Mr. Petric was exchanged on that occasion or whether he stayed behind?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Petric did not go on that occasion, nor was he ever exchanged later on. He accepted my suggestion, and he was taken back to Samac afterwards. And I think he continued to live in Samac afterwards, and he testified to this here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know that after this, Andrija Petric was released and allowed to go home?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was allowed to go home and he spent the whole time with his family. Of course, I know that the building in which he resided was hit by a shell and he had to move somewhere else, but I know he remained in Samac with his family throughout all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you tell us who, if anyone, of your family members arrived in that exchange from the territory of Odzak? Can you enumerate some names, if you can remember them.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among these names was my close relative, Savo Borojevic. There was also Svetozar Savic, my uncle. There was also Obrad Cajic, a relative of mine. There was Milan Arsenic, my uncle. And if I were to look at the exhibit, I might remember, but perhaps it's not so relevant now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When these relatives of yours arrived, what did you and Toso Tutnjevic do?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Toso and I took my relative, Savo Borojevic and some others in the car and we went with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went to Tekstilac, which is a canteen where the Red Cross, the local one from Samac, had organised the reception, so to say, of these people who had arrived from Odzak municipality to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, were you present at the exchange of the 4th of July, 1992, in Lipovac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, why you were present at this exchange which was held on the 4th of July, 1992, in Lipovac.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two very important reasons. One was because it so happened that I was seeing off friends of mine who were going to be exchanged, especially the Prgomet family, where my daughter Natasa is married to one of their family members, and some other friends related to that family. The second reason was that I had information that a large number of my nearest and dearest, my friends and relatives, would be arriving from Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did the Prgomet family ask you to see them off?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. My friend, so I call him, Djuro Prgomet, asked me if I could go with them to the place of exchange because there were about 30 relatives of his and his wife's on the list who had applied to the Red Cross, wishing to go to the territory of the Republic of Croatia, and they were afraid that something might happen and he would feel safer if I was with them. Of course, it never occurred to me to refuse my friend's request, and before this decision that he made to be exchanged, he had experienced some unpleasantness. He had been arrested by the police in Samac because he was a Croat. He had been detained in the school. Two men were killed in front of his eyes, and he was afraid, and that was why he wanted very much to leave the area with his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you say "friend," let's clarify this for the sake of the transcript. Whenever you use the word "friend, Djuro Prgomet," what in fact do you mean by this term "friend"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My daughter Natasa is married to his son. In our area, the parents of children who marry each other are referred to as friends. They're a special kind of friend. Djuro Prgomet is the father of my son-in-law, who married my daughter Natasa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe how you travelled from the house of Djuro Prgomet, your son-in-law's father, to the place of exchange?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the number of people who were exchanged on both sides was such that it was one of the largest exchanges, if not the largest, between the municipalities of Bosanski Samac and Odzak at the time. On that day, the 4th of July, I and my driver came to my friend's house, or rather, my relative's house. I helped them take their belongings and go to the playing field in front of the secondary school, where buses were prepared to take people to the exchange; not only them, but afterwards Toso went and collected the rest of the family, because, as I say, there were over 30 family members who had applied in the Red Cross, and some of them arrived on foot, but some of them had belongings to carry, so Toso went and drove them

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So they got on the buses, and then how did the exchange proceed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went through Bosanski Samac via Loncari, Brcko, Bijeljina, Race on the bank of the Sava, which divides Bosnia-Herzegovina from Serbia in that area, and then, when they crossed over to Serbia, they went in the direction of the town of Sid. And nearby is the village of Lipovac, where the international forces of UNPROFOR were stationed and where, on the 5th of July, the exchange took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: That convoy of buses that was involved in the exchange, was it subjected to any checks at various checkpoints? Were there any problems while crossing through those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were checkpoints. There weren't any major problems. The largest problem occurred at the Gorica checkpoint. The entire convoy was stopped there. I wish to say that on that occasion I went in my own private car, a Golf, and when the buses were stopped, I went out of my car and approached the spot to see what was it all about. One of the alleged commanders of that police patrol attacked fiercely, verbally, Mr. Miroslav Tadic, as well as people who were organisers of the exchange, because in one of the buses there was Mr. Grga Zubak, and the policemen believed that he shouldn't have been there because allegedly one could get a large number of people in exchange for him. So it was a tense situation that went on for several minutes, until he calmed down and let the convoy continue. Mr. Tadic and he had a fierce verbal duel before he finally conceded and let the convoy go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Grga Zubak remain on the bus?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He remained in the convoy, and I remember well that he also came to Sid where another unpleasant incident regarding him took place. Some people arrived there, and I can tell you now that it was pre-arranged by somebody else. How come Serbs from Vukovar knew that Grga Zubak was on that bus? They wanted to get him off the bus, and thanks to Mr. Tadic, Veljo Maslic, and Svetozar Vasovic, somebody else intervened and these three gentlemen that I mentioned were the official organisers of the exchange, and everybody knew that Grga Zubak was to be exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And was Grga Zubak finally exchanged on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Zaric, have any official assignment in that exchange that took place on the 4th of July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: None whatsoever, except what I mentioned in the beginning of my testimony, when I explained how it came about that I was present there during that exchange, because I was seeing some people off, some people that were very dear to me, and at the same time I was greeting some relatives of mine arriving from Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you ever a member of the exchange committee in Bosanski Samac municipality, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the municipal Red Cross, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us now return, Mr. Zaric, to the end of May, 1992. I wish to analyse with you two conversations that you had via the centre for information and with the people in Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we will be mentioning a protected witness, and therefore I suggest that we now turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, let us now move on and talk about late July 1992. It was not challenged that you then became an advisor in Odzak. So would you please first tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Pisarevic has to pose the question again, because his question was not: It was not challenged that you then became an advisor in Odzak. This is how -- what the record says, and maybe we should go through this again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I don't seem to understand the interjection, but can we proceed, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, the question of Mr. Pisarevic was that Mr. Zaric became deputy of the president of civilian war council in Odzak, and here it says advisor in Odzak. It's not accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. It's the translation. Can the question be repeated, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you assumed the duty in Odzak as deputy president of the civilian war council in Odzak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assistant, not deputy, an assistant to the president of the civil war council. The president had several assistants, and that's how we experienced this body. Nobody was officially his deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. First tell us: When was the municipality and town of Odzak put under the control of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in mid-July, around the 15th of July, when the forces of the 1st Krajina Corps took the municipality of Odzak under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of this military operation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was entitled "Corridor."

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know which military formation of the army of Republika Srpska took part in Operation Corridor?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were mostly units from the 1st Krajina Corps. As far as I can recall, headed by the then commander, General Omer Talic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter corrects herself. Momir Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the 2nd Posavina Brigade took part in this operation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 2nd Posavina Brigade did not take part in the operations around Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that after Odzak was put under the control of the army of Republika Srpska, in the Odzak municipality, and therefore in the town of Odzak, a military administration was introduced?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what this meant in practice and what you understand by the term "military administration"?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the term "military administration," I understand a hierarchy of authority in the area, and the word "military administration" in this context means that the chief power was in the hands of the military administration, headed by the superior officer in charge of that area of responsibility where the military administration was introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zaric, do you know how it came about that the civilian war council was established for the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, this was perhaps a few days after the 1st Krajina Corps took control of the territory of Odzak, and a meeting was held in the office of the Crisis Staff in Samac, to which I was also invited. Mr. Blagoje Simic was there, as the president of the Crisis Staff; Milan Simic was there; Savo Popovic; Mr. Bozo Ninkovic, who at that time was already the chief of the department of the ministry of National Defence; and there was also a group of people who were born on the territory of Odzak municipality, some of whom had lived there before, and others had lived there in the municipality of Samac, but they originated from the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what was said to you at that meeting? Why were you invited there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Mr. Blagoje Simic, as the president of the Crisis Staff, informed us that a military person from the area of Odzak municipality had been to see him. I think this man's name was also Simic. And he was in charge of certain civilian affairs in the Krajina Corps or in that military administration - I'm not sure which - but Mr. Blagoje said that they had come to meet Mr. Simic and that a military administration had been introduced there. But because Samac was the municipality closest to Odzak and most of the Serbian people from Odzak municipality had become refugees in Samac and been given refugee status, all this gave me to understand that there was concern about the municipality of Odzak, political or humane concern, by the institutions in Samac. And then Mr. Blagoje said that they were asking the Crisis Staff to try and trace a number of people who had been born in the municipality of Odzak or had resided there, or residing in this area, and who might perhaps assist the civilian war council in order to establish normal life there, because there were no other people living in that area at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that there is some misunderstanding about what Mr. Zaric has just said. On page 72, when he was talking about people who were born in the municipality of Odzak or had resided there, or resided in this area, and who might perhaps assist the civilian war council in order to establish normal life there. He was referring to the military organs, not civilian war council. It wasn't established yet, obviously, at that point. He was referring to military administration that was already established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Zaric can go over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, could you please slow down and explain and answer this question as to the purpose of gathering these people together, whom they were supposed to assist, and so on.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Blagoje Simic informed us that this military person had asked him to have a civilian military body established, composed of people who had been born on the territory of the municipality of Odzak, regardless of whether they had been residing there or whether they were residing somewhere in the municipality of Samac, and the purpose of this was that the military administration, which had already been established there, should be assisted in establishing normal civilian life in the area. That's what I understood at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was this civilian war council in Odzak established then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people who were present at the meeting came up with suggestions. For example, Miso Pavic, from Novi Grad; and Andrija Jovanovic from Donja Dubica; and Mr. Milosevic from Donja Dubica, and a certain Goranovic from Trnjak. Spontaneously a suggestion was put forward that the president of this civilian war council should be me. Mr. Blagoje Simic responded to this by saying that he understood the suggestions of these people and that he personally was not opposed to this, but in view of some official connotations --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: As said by the witness.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Mr. Savo Popovic should be appointed to that post because he was a member of the Crisis Staff and could therefore establish direct communication with the Executive Board and the organs on the territory of Samac municipality. I was neither in the government, nor was I a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I did not respond to what he said, and I said as far as I was concerned there was no problem. It was agreed, however, that Mr. Zaric should go there and help, as far as he was able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what was your post in late July 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I was assistant commander of the 5th Infantry Battalion for intelligence and security and moral guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, at that meeting did you become part of that civilian war council for the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A general suggestion was made at that meeting by some of the participants, and the entire civilian war council was not nominated at that meeting. This was worked out later on in the course of practical work in the field. But a certain number of members were appointed at that time, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, during his testimony, Mr. Zaric, of course, in a number of occasions, mentioned this body that he was a member of, and he used to refer to it as civilian military council, not civilian war council. Word "war" was never mentioned. So maybe these words should be used further in the transcript, and this is actually the very same body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: This body, this civilian military council, this is the same body which was headed by Savo Popovic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So we use the term "civilian military council," then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you became part of the civilian military council, what tasks were you given and what were your duties in this civilian military council?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very soon after this, we went to the municipality of Odzak, and in a room in the hotel which had a sliding door and which was used as a dining-room, and when the sliding door was opened, it was partitioned off so that a smaller room was created. This was the first office used by the civilian military council in the hotel in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you arrived in Odzak, was the first session of the civilian military council held?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was held in the room I have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, can you remember who presided at that session and who was present?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The session was chaired by Colonel Novica Simic, who was then the commander of the Operative Group, which had the status of a military administration. And in my view, he was practically the military governor at that moment. Apart from him, from the military there was the chief of staff of the Operative Group, Major Mile Deronja; there was Mr. Mackic, who was the assistant for intelligence and security in the Operative Group and the military administration; then there was Colonel Dujanin, who was performing the duty of the assistant commander for the rear in the area; and among those of us who were from the civilian military council, there were about 10 or 15 of us approximately, there was Savo Popovic, of course, as the president of the civilian military council; there was Rajkica or Rajko Dragic, there was Mr. Jovanovic, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Nedic, Mr. Pavic, Mr. -- I think his name was -- I don't know what it was. A man who was in charge of health care. But at any rate, those were some of the people who I remember well as being members of that civilian military council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: At the first session of the civilian military council in Odzak, which was attended by the commander, Colonel Simic, what did Colonel Simic say? What was the relationship between the military administration and the civilian military council?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Colonel Simic said that on the territory of Odzak municipality, in the whole area of responsibility, a military administration had been introduced, and even further afield, because it also covered part of the territorial which was then under the control of these forces but which gravitated toward the municipality of Bosanski Brod. He said that he was pleased that we were all there, that he saw in us people who could help in the municipality of Odzak to create, as soon as possible, the conditions for the return of the refugees who had left Odzak while it was controlled by HVO forces. He pointed out that a military administration is rarely introduced but that this time it was a necessity and that it required a lot of discipline, order, work, and obedience, or words to that effect. And he said that it was up to the civilian military council now to nominate commissioners in the local communes, where we were expecting the return of refugees, to appoint commissioners in some companies in the town of Odzak, where all the industry of Odzak was concentrated, and also to appoint commissioners in other social institutions, in the health care system, the educational system, the utilities company, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And did the civilian military council assign tasks and appoint commissioners for certain areas of activity or certain towns and villages? Was this done?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was done. And all the proposals we put forward at that time, for example, who could be the commissioner in a company such as Energoinvest, Elkroj, so on, or in the town of Odzak. Each such decision was signed, apart from Mr. Todorovic, also by the commander of the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Which Todorovic did you mean?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant Popovic, Mr. Popovic, the president of the civilian military council. So that each decision was signed by the command of the military administration, and it also bore the stamp of the military administration, appointing certain people to certain duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, is it now time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will continue at 1445 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pisarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, before our break, we spoke about the appointment of various commissioners, and you told us that each of the appointments made by the civilian military council was further confirmed by the commander, who was at the helm of the military administration. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: What was your post within the civilian military council, and what were your duties and tasks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was assistant to the president of the civilian military council for security matters. That was the simplest way of defining it. Whereas the essence of my task in the hierarchy had to do with Mr. Gojko Mackic, who was the security officer of the military administration in Odzak. I received tasks and assignments directly from him, and I reported directly to him, so to speak, or rather, everything that I found out that had to do with the security, I conveyed to him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you said that you reported directly to him, do you mean that you submitted certain reports to him about your work?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did submit reports to him about my work, about what I had learned while working in the field; and if I made any official notes, memos, or conducted any official interviews with the persons while working in Odzak municipality, then I would transmit to him the written material concerning that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you conducted certain informative interviews in Odzak municipality and also compiled official notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the usher to help me with the document, which has our internal marking PDB 8/4. If one copy could be placed on the ELMO, please, or rather, if one copy could be put in front of Mr. Zaric.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask that one copy be placed on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please take a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The interpreters requested that one copy be placed on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It has been, Your Honour. Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Have you looked at it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Is that an official note on the informative interview conducted with Drago Rakic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is, an official note on informative interview conducted with Drago Rakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now please take a look at the last page of the document. Is the signature of the person conducting the interview, or rather, drafting up the official note, your signature?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read to us what it says above your signature.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above my signature it says: "Assistant to the president of the military council for security matters," and then underneath it says: "Simo Zaric," and you can see that I personally signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Was that your official title, the one that you've just read to us?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly what my official post was. And now that we're dealing with the term "official note," I would like to explain that it's not a typical statement, but rather an official note. And if you can take a look at the last sentence, which is right above my signature, it says there: "I suggest that the intelligence security organ for the area of Trnjak conduct an additional clarifying interview with Rakic and suggest further operative measures. This is what I suggested concerning Rakic and then the rest was up to the people who were within the military administration in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you drafted this official note, what did you do with it actually?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave this official note to Mr. Gojko Mackic, who was the chief security officer for the entire area of responsibility within the military administration in Odzak municipality. In the area of Trnjak, which I mention here, there was a part of the unit of Laktasi Brigade, where there was kept in Jez for a time a security officer. Therefore, I suggested that that security officer should conduct further clarifying interview, because Mr. Rakic returned back to his home and lived in the area of responsibility of that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't need that document any more. Thank you. Could we please be given a number for this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to be clear with you, Mr. Pisarevic. You wanted this document in as an example of the type of work Mr. Simo Zaric used to perform at that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Including what he did at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Any objection from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be treated as Exhibit D52/4 and D52/4 ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to introduce additional two documents which are identical, and all of the questions that had been put so far with respect to the previous document would also apply to these two documents. So perhaps we could just put this before Mr. Zaric to see if this is indeed his signature. These documents have internal number PDB 9/4 and PDB 10/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, have you looked at this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. This is a document drafted by me. This is my signature at the end of the document. And there is also a proposal to undertake certain measures.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: This document is an official note that you drafted after conducting an informative interview with Rajko Vujkovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. This is an official note which I compiled while conducting the interview with Rajko Vukovic. I would like to say that when it comes to methodology in compiling this official note, that what is most important to me is the content of the official note and how I conveyed to the security officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, all right. That is the most important thing for you. But now we are focusing on what was your job during that time while you were in Odzak, for one month, and the question speaks for itself about your work.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown, please, document PDB 10/4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, please take a look. Please put it on the ELMO. Have you -- did you compile this document, Mr. Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This is an official note following my conducting an interview, informative interview, with Borislav Rakic. At the end of this document there is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't be needing these documents any more. Thank you. Could these documents be marked, please, as exhibits. Could they be admitted into evidence, please, and be given numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the numbers? I take it the Prosecution holds the same stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, we've got the same documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The official note dated 31st of July, 1992, will be Exhibit D53/4 and ter for the B/C/S. The official note dated 3rd of August, 1992, will be Exhibit D54/4 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, we have seen here three official notes. Did you compile any other similar official notes?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a great number of them. And when I say "a great number," I mean tens of them, dozens of them. And they focused on the issues that were covered in the official notes that we have seen here. Some of my interviews were conducted with some of the residents of Odzak municipality who happened to be either in the camps or happened to stay in Odzak municipality. They experienced certain things. And then, together with the rest of the documentation I could get a hold of, I would turn that and this documentation to the security officer. I know for a fact that some of the documents were sent to the committee for investigating war crimes in Belgrade, which was then transmitted to the International Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards all of the official notes compiled by you, did you compile them and treat them in the same way as these three that we have analysed here, or rather, who did you send this to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The methodology was the same. I would compile up an official note, then I would submit it to Mr. Gojko Mackic. During that one month while I stayed in Odzak municipality, he was the chief security officer of the military administration for the entire area of responsibility in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you submit any kind of reports to the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac municipality? Or rather, at that time, that was the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have such a duty, neither did anybody assign that duty to me, nor did I ever submit any kind of written reports to the Crisis Staff in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you receive any orders from the War Presidency of Bosanski Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not receive any orders. There is something peculiar there with respect to all other members of the civilian military council. The office of the Ministry of Defence of Bosanski Samac assigned me to a unit which had a number within that military administration. Therefore, that month that I spent there is recorded in my records as me being there as a member of the military administration and working as a security officer in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, while you discharged these duties in the municipality of Odzak and in the town itself, did you have some kind of an office? Did you have a working space; and if so, where was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My working space was a desk in a corner of the large room that was created by closing the sliding door when the sessions of the civilian military council were held. In the evening hours, or whenever I had any time available, I would go to that desk and type up written material. Therefore, I did not have adequate working conditions which are required or were required by the nature of my work. However, such were the circumstances in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what kind of technical equipment was at your disposal in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had nothing but a typing machine, some paper, pens, and an old briefcase that I used to carry around with me and that was used as evidence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Sorry. Excuse me, Mr. Pisarevic. Just for the sake of clarity, I'd like to just ask Mr. Zaric one question. Mr. Zaric, you mentioned here the old briefcase, and it's stated here, quoting you, that "I used to carry around with me and that was used as evidence here." I'd just like to point out that when we looked at a briefcase here and the Judges examined it here on the Bench, it was not the actual briefcase that you were using then, but rather the briefcase that you bring into Court every day. Am I correct? We didn't see the actual old briefcase. What was put before us was the briefcase that you bring into Court every day, and we looked at that as an example of the type of briefcase that you were using then, and I believe a photocopy was made of it off the ELMO. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, you're not correct. That briefcase which was photographed here is the very same briefcase that I had before the war. It is at least 20 years old, and that was the only briefcase I used, both during the events in Samac and while I was in Odzak discharging this task. I don't think there's anything contentious here. I still carry that very briefcase today. I bring my papers in it when I come here to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I realise that, Mr. Zaric, and we see it every day. It was just that my recollection - I stand to be corrected - my recollection was that we were looking at that briefcase just as an example of the same type. But if you say that it is the same one that you were using and have used for 20 years, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's precisely right, Your Honour. This is the briefcase that I've been using for over 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, you said that the civilian military council, upon approval of the commander of the military administration, appointed commissioners for certain economic subjects and for certain inhabited places. Can you please tell us: Who was appointed by the civilian military council and the military administration commissioner in the town of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the town of Odzak, Mr. Dusko Gavric was appointed commissioner. I remember some other commissioners in various local communes. For example, in Donja Dubica, Minic, Aco, was appointed commissioner. In Trnjak, it was Ljubo Goranovic. In Svilaj, it was Mr. Rakic. In Novi Grad, it was Drago Nedic. So I remember some people from that time who acted both as commissioners in local communes, and I remember that Mr. Gavric was commissioner in the town of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who was appointed commissioner in certain economic subjects, in certain companies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, I think, if I recall correctly, we heard most of this evidence from Mr. Savo Popovic, and I don't think that we're interested in repeating it. I think Mr. Zaric can stick to what role he played at that time. I think we had enough covered as to how the administration was run there, from Mr. Savo Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We will not dwell on that any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when you came to Odzak for the first time, what did you see there, or rather, what was the situation like in town?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The town was not in a particularly good situation. Several large residential buildings had burnt down. For example, in a new settlement called Hanka, which was not far from the gym hall and secondary school in Odzak, one of the largest residential buildings in downtown Odzak, not far from the market, had also burnt down, and there were a number of houses that were either torched or mined. And there was a large number of buildings that were not damaged by shelling or anything else. So I believe that the situation as I found it indicated that there had been military operations going on, that a lot of damage was created by the withdrawal of the HVO, and that a lot of buildings were damaged. That was the situation in the Odzak area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Upon your arrival, did you find any civilian population in Odzak, the town and the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no population whatsoever, except a small number of Serbs who were hiding in forests, or elsewhere, during the pull-out of the HVO forces. Those were the only residents we found when we arrived in Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, do you know whether, in Odzak municipality, in town, there were any civilians of Croat and Muslim ethnicity at the time of your arrival?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived there, I did not find any Croats or Muslims there, nor did anybody say that there were any residents who were of that ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, prior to your arrival in Odzak, was a detachment of civilian police from Samac already deployed there in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember who was the commander of that detachment of police from Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander of that police detachment was Mirko Pavic, who prior to that used to work as a policeman. He was a professional policeman in Bosanski Samac. Mr. Mirko Pavic was born in Novi Grad in Odzak municipality, and that was perhaps one of the reasons for his appointment for a time as commander of the police station in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall perhaps how many civilian policemen and which civilian policemen were in that particular police unit from Bosanski Samac sent to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't really remember most of their names, but I know well last names of some men. And even Mr. Gavric was in the early days a policeman, the one who became a commissioner later on. So one was Ugljesic; one was Rakic, who came from Novi Grad; there was one Milojevic, from Donja Dubica; Kovacevic, from Novi Grad. I remember those guys, but there were also some others whom I did not know all that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Were there any checkpoints at places, at accesses to the area of the military administration?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To be quite honest, during the war, in a small area, I've never seen more checkpoints in a smaller area of the municipality than in the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Problem in the transcript. The answer was not no, as recorded on page 88, line 18. Mr. Zaric started his sentence with: "Never," and then he continued saying that never in one -- in a smaller place were more checkpoints. And here is recorded "no." So actually it is an opposite answer that Mr. Zaric gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can that be -- can you go over that so that we get the correct answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did you understand what the problem is? Will you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To make it clear, there was a very large number of checkpoints in the municipality of Odzak. Every unit which made part of the military administration had its own checkpoint and some sort of its area of responsibility. So that it was a psychological burden in the early days to have to go through all those checkpoints. If one went from Odzak to Novi Grad, or to Trnjak, which was my birth place, one had to go through no less than 10 or 15, all sorts of different checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And who was at those checkpoints? Who manned them?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At those checkpoints, in the depth of the territory, were the members of the units. At times, they had belts and looked like military police, and in places there were ordinary soldiers without those white belts. So that you enter an area, you come across a checkpoint, and they were authorised to stop you, to check you, and everybody had to produce a relevant paper showing that he was permitted to move in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you and other members of that civilian military council, or persons in general who came to the area of the military administration in Odzak, was everybody bound to have a permit to enter -- to gain access?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, down to the last one. You couldn't move about without those permits. We were members of that body, and it just so happened that I was a man who was frequently on the ground, in the field, yet I couldn't go anywhere without being stopped, and I had to show my pass that I had been issued by the military administration so that I could move around the area of responsibility, the territory of the Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you please explain the procedure. What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will the counsel and the witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the soldier stops you at the checkpoint, for me and my driver, I was driven at the time by Mr. Tutnjevic and asked to see our IDs. And then I show a pass which says that Mr. Simo Zaric is authorised to move around the area of responsibility in the territory of the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you slow down, Mr. Zaric, please. Mr. Zaric, who was responsible to take care of the infrastructure and normalisation of living conditions in the town of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All this aspect of life that was being made to suit more normal civilisational conditions was the responsibility of Mr. Dusan Gavric, who assigned a team of people that he would cooperate with so that he could perform all the jobs that had to do with infrastructure and everything else which was indispensable for a normal life.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, did citizens who were under labour obligation come to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of what ethnic group did they belong to, those citizens who came to Odzak under labour obligation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those citizens came from the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac and were by and large Muslims and Croats, from the territory of the municipality of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which means of transportation, in what way did they get from Bosanski Samac to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, at times they took buses, but more often than not they would be brought in by trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did they have any escort?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was mandatory, in addition to a driver, there would always be a policeman from the public security station, invariably, either when they came by bus or when they came by truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what was the procedure for people under labour obligation to make these people take these means of transportation to come to Odzak? Where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I could see and hear, because that was not my field, they would fetch up in front of the police station's building more often than not, in Odzak, I mean, and it is more or less in the centre of the town, about three to four hundred metres away from the hotel and the military administration command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was there to receive them, or who would be there to receive them?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be received there by the commissioner from Odzak, and they would fetch up in front of the public security station, and then, from there, they were assigned to various tasks and jobs which the commissioner had agreed with the president of the civilian military council or the military administration, depending on what had to be done or what had most urgently to be settled at that particular moment in the territory of the town of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, to the best of your recollection, who issued tasks to those people who were under labour obligation, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was Mr. Gavric, the commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you, Mr. Zaric, were those people who were under labour obligation under any kind of your jurisdiction or not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I absolutely had no authority over those people, nor was I in a position to issue any orders to these people, that is, to do whatever. It went beyond my tasks and beyond the needs of my service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine. And, Mr. Zaric, during your stay in Odzak, did you have an opportunity to see those people who were under labour obligation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw -- I would see them as I would walk down a street, and people worked. And now it depends. Some swept streets, some mended roofs. I saw women sweeping streets or putting the hotel in order, or who worked in the kitchen, so that at times that segment of the work happened before my eyes, and that is where I would see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever control the work of people under labour obligation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never did that. There was no need for me to do that. And in that hotel that I'm mentioning, there was a joint kitchen, a canteen, for everybody who had their meals there. So that on several occasions, I had the opportunity to sit together with them, and I deliberately at times moved -- changed tables so as to be with everybody. For a while, it was merely concerning personal relations and so on and so forth. But I know they had the same meals as we did, that is, as other people who had some other commitments and tasks in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, within the framework of your jurisdiction, were you in a position to protect some of the people under labour obligation in Odzak? I, in particular, mean women, persons of the female gender.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once I had the opportunity, as I was working in that room in Odzak, I was approached by a young woman. She happened to be related to my wife. And she complained to me of the vulgar behaviour of a soldier from Krajina who insisted that she should go with him to some special room, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So what did you do when you heard it from her?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I heard about it, I notified Mr. Mackic, and I know well that Mr. Mackic took certain steps, and I think later on he talked with all those women, once when they were at lunch there, and said: If you have problems of this kind, to let him know immediately. And after his admonition, I think that a similar intervention never happened again, and I do not think that anyone ever asked assistance because something like that was happening to her. But I -- yes, but this incident stuck in my memory because I personally interceded with Mr. Mackic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, are you aware that property was taken away from Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell us: What was the procedure? If somebody wanted to take some property from the territory of Odzak, or rather, from the territory controlled by that military administration?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know well what people in the military administration told us at a meeting we had concerning property, that it could not be taken out of the area without relevant certificates which could only be issued by the military administration. However, what I could see in practice, and what I could learn in practice, is that there was a big gap between what was theoretically advocated and verbally advocated and the manifestations this phenomenon took in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. Zaric. Will you please tell me: If somebody wants to take out some movable property, who is it that one has to apply to for the authorisation to take out this movable property from the municipality of Odzak? What was the procedure to follow?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure was: If it was necessary to take out some goods from the territory of Odzak, then one had to have the authorisation issued by the military administration, that is, without the signature or whether the assistant commander for the logistics, which was part of the military administration, or another authorised person, authorised by the commander of the military administration, that is, and that the application could then be submitted. And if it had to do with the civilian sector, then such an application could be made by Mr. Savo Popovic, on behalf of the civilian military council. If some of the goods -- if some merchandise was to be taken to some other area or if somebody needed to take something private from an area, again, one had to have the authorisation of the relevant military administration. So without this document, and that was a rule which had -- which had been made public, nobody should have been allowed to take anything out without having it put on record and without knowing the destination of that merchandise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you well, no merchandise and no property could leave the territory of the municipality of Odzak without the knowledge of the military administration.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That is how I understood that. And I believe that certain documents which I saw by accident always bore the signature of the person authorised by the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us: How was the control performed? That is, that all the merchandise or all the movable property was accompanied by appropriate documentation, how could that be checked?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say something in all honesty. I'm not defending the position of Odzak or something that went on only in the municipality of Samac or Odzak. During this unfortunate war -- this unfortunate war was particularly characteristic of the general criminalisation which was related both to people and the army. What happened in Odzak, even though there was a military administration there. For instance, I received information from some policemen that at the checkpoint, some of the merchandise, some of the goods, with a signature of authority had left in the direction of Krajina and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, will you please answer just this one question: What were the measures which -- what were the measures attempted to be put in order in order to enforce the decision? And we shall discuss criminal removable property at some other time.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was these checkpoints which were at all the main exits from Odzak. One led towards the municipality of Modrica, another one into the depth of the municipality at the time of the pontoon bridge across the River Bosna, one went in the direction of Samac, and the third one went through Novi Grad, towards the municipality of Brod. So these were the three exits, and one couldn't leave the municipality of Odzak without coming across those checkpoints, at which one could check whether there was documentation accompanying all the merchandise, all the movables that were being taken out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me: In your opinion, were the movables taken out disregarding the procedure prescribed for the municipality of Odzak and from the territory of the military administration?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd say yes. It did happen, and one couldn't keep it all under control. I cannot say that it happened tacitly, but it looked to me as if somebody tolerated a part of such phenomena.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pisarevic, this answer doesn't help us at all. Actually, I think it's as a result of your own question, where you asked the witness whether in his opinion. What you should be asking him is what actually happened, what did he see, if anything, regarding this -- the property movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was what I was driving at with my question, but perhaps I wasn't precise enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what it is that you know, what did you see, that is, and what information did you receive while you stayed and worked in Odzak about illegal, wrongful, illicit removal of property from the territory of Odzak, that is, the town of Odzak? What do you know, if you know anything about it? Will you tell the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To begin with, I will say that when we made our first steps as the civilian military council, one of our first tasks was -- and I think we did it very properly indeed - we made a register of all the property found in companies and private business outlets in the territory of the town and municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, will you please make a pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could D49/4 be shown to the witness. That is the register of property in the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, will you please have a look at the document. Leaf through it to see what it's about, and especially I want you to look at the last page to see who signed the document. Have you had a look?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. It is the document that I was talking about. Well, it says here "the military council." It's some initial terminology, insufficient for those early days, and it was signed by Rajko Dervenic, who was assistant president of the civilian council for economic affairs for the municipality of Odzak. That was the definition of the office he held in this civilian military council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, as a member of that commission which made a census of all the property that we see in this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it just happened that I participated in this census during the first two days, and I was at the Borovo [Realtime transcript read in error "Boro"] Factory and the Elkroj factory, and the report and the census we submitted together, and it had been incorporated in this one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of this factory, Borovo -- what was it? Because it's misspelled in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is under Roman VIII on page 5 of the Bijic [phoen] version, Borovo Odzak - Odzak, that is one company, and the other one is a company which is under Roman VII, it is called Elkroj Odzak 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So you are referring to two companies in which you personally participated in the census in the taking of the stock?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with some other people who were with me in that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Right. We don't need this document any longer. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It transpires quite clearly from the document that some economic facilities were unscathed and undamaged at the time when the territory of Odzak was taken over by Serb forces, or rather, by the 1st Krajina Corps and introduction of the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, what was the purpose of this document?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, its purpose was to take stock of the situation and to try to see whether prerequisites could be provided for the re-activation of normal business life in the territory of the municipality of Odzak. That was the chief purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what do you know about it? Were these facilities preserved and all these assets that you registered, that you recorded, or rather, Mr. Rajko, when you did this in the beginning, when the civilian military council came to Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some of these assets, yes, have been preserved, and others had been taken away in different ways, I'd say using both civilian and military channels, from the municipality of Odzak. I can give you a few characteristic examples on the basis of which the Chamber could see how I perceived and experienced this problem. When referring to the Elkroj factory and the Borovo factory, I know that with some documentation, the machinery from that factory, the machines from that factory were taken by trucks to the factory of Utva in the territory of the Bosanski Samac municipality. I happened to see those machines in that warehouse with my own eyes. So they had been transferred from those factories and brought over there. And what was the lot of these machines after that, and where they went on, that I do not know. Perhaps some bodies will go into that at some stage. The second question: I've told you about my orchard in Trnjak. At that time, the fruit trees had been felled. But this orchard was fenced off with a metal fence. Hundreds of heads -- when I say "heads," I mean livestock, all sorts of, from the youngest calves to yearlings to cows, and on, they had all been put into this compound, into my orchard. And the first time I got to that village, those commissioners had practically got together this livestock which was wandering around, they had rounded up all this cattle and put it in that orchard. And the cattle stayed there for a while, they fed it, and ate it, and after that they gave back to the troops and the rest of the cattle I know was transferred with the consent of the military administration. Some of it was taken to the municipality of Samac with their authorisation. And then the Executive Board of the municipality of Samac then distributed it to different farms, and so on and so forth. So that is what I know. I also know that one of the most expensive machines at the Strolit factory had been taken away upon the order of the social military administration, that is, the military administration which was duty-bound until after that, yet they allowed that a very expensive machine go to Jelsingrad and I heard that it had been installed there to meet the needs of some other factory over there. And in Donja Dubica the troops from Krajina savaged and destroyed a completely new telephone exchange which had been put up in Donja Dubica. So when I mentioned a word, when I said there was organised, as I called it, plunder, that is what I had in mind. To my mind, it wasn't sufficient to have a document that some merchandise could be taken out if it was being alienated from a particular source or political account community, and yet we are getting ready to introduce in that area a new civilised life and bring in our people who were refugees at the time. So that was my very rigorous attitude to this subject and I did not spare either side when I say this. But again, what went to Samac again could not go there without somebody having initialed and approved such a thing. When I say "someone," I mean somebody in the military administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment ago you mentioned the one side and the other side. What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the military, if they were alienating and taking away some goods or if a truck arrived in front of the Samac Executive Board driving that livestock, or if machines were removed, I was then referring to the Executive Board, representing the authorities in Samac. And of course the question arises as to what the fate of the machines and the equipment was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: So when you say "both sides," one side, according to you, is the civilian authority and the other one is the military?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, while you were in Odzak, did you spend the nights there?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't spend the nights in Odzak. I often stayed in Odzak throughout the day. But every evening I went back to Bosanski Samac with Mr. Tutnjevic and slept either in my own flat or, depending on the security situation, somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Toso go from Samac to Odzak and come back every day?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't a long drive, because when the platoon bridge -- the pontoon bridge was set up near the village of Pisari, over the River Sava, we could go between Samac and Odzak in about 15 minutes. It's only 15 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, while you were in Odzak municipality and in the town of Odzak, was your sister Jelena there, and what did she do in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One of my sisters who had lived in Odzak before the war was Jelena, and when the civilian military council started its work, she acted as a secretary in the civilian military council, and she was actually the technical secretary of Mr. Savo Popovic for the issuing of documents, certificates, or any other documents within his competence. And later on, Jelena went to work in the local Red Cross on the territory of Odzak municipality, and she worked there as a clerk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, while you were in Odzak, did you ever appropriate any property belonging to somebody else from Odzak, thus gaining possessions, material possessions, property, profiting by this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I like to refer to sayings, and I'm now referring to one which means that I never took anything, nor did it ever occur to me to do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, while you were in Odzak for about a month or so, was Savo Popovic the president of the civilian military council throughout this time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, and when I left around the 25th of August, he stayed on. I left Odzak as soon as the new commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade was appointed. I was called back and practically a few days before the end of August I left Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Toso Tutnjevic stay with you until the 25th of August? Did you leave Odzak together?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we left Odzak together. And on the 25th of August, I was called to the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade because in Pelagicevo a new commander had been appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that, Mr. Zaric. But tell me now: After this period of time, that is, after the 25th of August, 1992, did you go to the territory of Odzak municipality and to the town of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, mostly to my native village of Trnjak, where normal conditions were created. I went to try to repair some things so that my mother could return. She was a refugee. And I also went to Odzak to visit my sister Jelena, who was the only one of my sisters living there, because the property of my other sisters had been completely destroyed and they were never actually able to return to the territory of Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: To conclude: While you were in Odzak, what was your status? Were you a member of the military or were you a person with a work obligation?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the status of a military person. I was attached to the military command of the military administration, and I wish I had the document now, because I can't recall the number. But from the 25th of July to the 30th of August, my booklet says that I was a member of the Operative Group, which had its number. So that I was exclusively a member of the military. That's how I was treated. Although I have described how I came to Odzak and what I did there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Zaric, where did you go after the 25th of August, 1992, when, as you say, you left the territory of Odzak municipality and the territory of the Odzak military administration? Could you just wait a moment.

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed that I was to report to the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade in Pelagicevo on the 25th of August. I received this information through the duty officer in the communication centre, in the 5th Infantry Battalion. He rang me up in the evening and said that he had received this information. So that with my driver, Mr. Tutnjevic, instead of going to Odzak, in the morning I went to Pelagicevo to report to the command of the 2nd Posavina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: And what did they say to you there? To what duty did they assign you?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new commander told me - and that was Major Mile Beronja, who only a day or two before was appointed by the commander of the East Bosnian Corps to be the commander of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade. He told me I was appointed assistant commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade for moral guidance, religious, and legal matters. That was the title according to the establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zaric, when was this order issued by Commander Mile Beronja?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation with me was conducted in the presence of Commander Beronja and the Chief of Staff, Jondic, Vojislav, a captain first class, who was then performing the duty of Chief of Staff of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. I was told that I was to prepare for my transfer and the decision on my appointment to this duty was formally to begin on the 1st of September, 1992, when I began to live and work in the 2nd Posavina Brigade in Pelagicevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: When you said "to live," what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because for a time I resided, whenever it was necessary, in a building we had there, where, when you had completed your task and night fell, Mr. Tutnjevic was my driver and I had a room where we could stay, because the command required me to be present there in the command and on the ground. This was quite a different kind of duty, far more responsible than others I had performed before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you spent most of your time now in the village of Pelagicevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PISAREVIC
utterances.text: Can you now briefly try to explain: What was the sphere of competence of the organ for moral guidance, religious, and legal matters? What were the tasks of this organ in a brigade such as the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SIMO ZARIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I wish to say: Unfortunately, before I was appointed to that duty, there was no one else. I had no predecessor to hand over to me documents and suchlike. But the chief duty was to maintain direct contact with the units on the ground, understand the mood of the soldiers, understand their material and social status, to help the families of wounded soldiers or soldiers who had been killed, take care of funerals, deal with their status. So this was a social card --
